text:
The University of Chicago was founded in 1890 as a coeducational institution by the American Baptist Education Society, supplemented by donations from John D. Rockefeller and land from Marshall Field. Its early history includes the closure of the Old University of Chicago in 1886 due to financial struggles. Under its early presidents, William Rainey Harper and Harry Pratt Judson, the university established its structure, adopting a quarter system, and the Divinity School in 1891.
Significant academic and intellectual developments occurred throughout its history, including the emergence of the Chicago Schools of thought in the social sciences. Robert Maynard Hutchins became president in 1929, implementing the "New Plan," a two-year general education curriculum that formed the basis for the university's core curriculum. The university's research contributions include the site of the Chicago Pile-1 (the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction) and the development of radiocarbon dating by Willard F. Libby. In 2021, the university's president was succeeded by Paul Alivisatos.
